text_html: A 50-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after he was involved in a motor vehicle collision. He reports difficulty breathing, chest pain, and pain in his right hand and leg. His temperature is 37°C (98.7°F), pulse is 124/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a laceration above the left eye and distention of the neck veins. The lungs are clear. Heart sounds are muffled. Palpation of the dorsal right wrist produces pain. The patient is unable to bear weight on the right lower extremity, and there is moderate swelling of the right ankle. The extremities are cool to the touch. His hemoglobin concentration is 13.5 g/dL, and hematocrit is 40%. X-rays show fractures of the scaphoid and distal radius in the right upper extremity and a tibial plateau fracture in the right lower extremity. Which of the following changes in systolic blood pressure is most likely in this patient?
explanation_html:
Educational Objective: For this patient presenting with traumatic injuries, the findings of hypotension, jugular venous distension, and muffled heart sounds is most suggestive of cardiac tamponade. Pulsus paradoxus is a decrease in systolic blood pressure >10 mm Hg with inspiration and will be present in this patient with cardiac tamponade.

Evaluation: Cardiac tamponade classically presents with hypotension, jugular venous distension, and muffled heart sounds. Patients often are tachycardic and have pulsus paradoxus (systolic blood pressure decreasing greater than 10 mm Hg with inspiration) on physical examination.

Definition: Cardiac tamponade is a life-threatening condition where fluid builds up in the pericardial sac and compresses the heart, preventing it from filling properly. This decreased filling leads to decreased cardiac output and can quickly cause shock if not treated. Echocardiography showing an echo-free space within the pericardium would be consistent with pericardial effusion; however, cardiac tamponade occurs when there is hemodynamic compromise secondary to fluid accumulation. Cardiac tamponade is a clinical diagnosis when there is evidence of right ventricular diastolic collapse and respiratory variation of cardiac output.

Prevention: Prevention of trauma to the chest would prevent cardiac tamponade in this patient.

Treatment: Treatment for cardiac tamponade involves immediate management with pericardiocentesis and then treatment of the underlying condition that caused cardiac tamponade.

Differential: The differential diagnosis for a patient who sustained trauma with hemodynamic compromise after injury is broad. This differential narrows with a thorough physical examination, x-rays, and laboratory studies. This patient has cardiac tamponade and will most likely have pulsus paradoxus on examination.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Choices A, C, D, and E: Decrease >10 mm Hg with expiration, increase >10 mm Hg with expiration, increase >10 mm Hg with inspiration, and no change with inspiration are incorrect. Cardiac tamponade results in pulsus paradoxus, which is decrease of systolic blood pressure greater than 10 mm Hg with inspiration.
